turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning. You're in room two whenever you're ready. Your sister's been on the phone answering the questions for you. She said you've been vomiting all morning and the cheek's been up for a week.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): She shouldn't answer for me. I have not been vomiting, not once. And it's not a week. Umm, sorry.
[SEG0003] person_2 (PATIENT): The telly out there is so loud I can't hear myself think. Are you running late?
[SEG0004] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Ten minutes, give or take. The nurse will do your obs first.
[SEG0005] person_3 (NURSE): In you come. My sister had a crown last year and she lived on soup, so I do feel for you. Blood pressure is 132 over 84, pulse 96, temperature 37.8, sats 98 percent.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 37.8 bad? I get panicky with numbers.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Shah. 37.8 is only a mild temperature, nothing dangerous on its own. What's brought you in?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the tooth. Well, the cheek. I had a crown on the upper right one on Thursday, and now that side of my face has blown up and the tooth's throbbing. I feel like a wet rag.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): When did the face come up?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Three days. The pain started Saturday. Well actually I thought Friday night, no, Saturday. My sister just guesses.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mm. Reception has a week from your sister, and you've got three days. I won't force it. Call it roughly three days to a week.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): It's throbbing, like a little hammer in the tooth. And I've overdone it, I had toast and that made it miles worse.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever with it?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): A mild one. I was hot last night. At home this morning it was 37.8, same as just now, not a high one.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any trouble swallowing, or with your breathing?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Swallowing's alright. Breathing's fine. I'm just frightened it'll turn.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, frog in my throat, I'm nervous. Is my face going to stay like this? I look a right state.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): It shouldn't stay like this. Let me have a look, then I'll talk you through what I think.

[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right cheek is swollen, warm and tender when I press. The gum by that crowned upper right molar is red. No collection I can feel. Mouth opens fine and the airway looks alright.

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it an abscess then? The dentist can't see me till next week, they're away. I've been on paracetamol, err, two grams, no, one gram four times a day, by mouth. The naproxin I stopped in March, the GP took me off it.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Naproxen, yes, leave that stopped. Did the dentist actually give you anything else?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): He talked about metronidazole. He never gave it to me though, I never took a single one. Should I have picked it up from the chemist?
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): No need. A medicine you never had isn't one we count. Any allergies, penicillin or anything else?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. No allergies.

[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Throbbing pain, swollen cheek, low-grade temperature, coming on after the crown. I think this is an early dental abscess. The swelling is your body fighting the infection round the root, so the tissue inflames and the cheek fills up. I don't think it has tracked into the neck.

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): So the tablets can hold it even if he can't drain it? What if I'm worse tonight, I keep picturing my throat closing. And can I work, I've got a shift at the bakery tomorrow?

[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, they can hold a local infection until the dentist sees you. I'll prescribe amoxicillin, 500 milligrams, three times a day, for five days, by mouth. Start today and finish the course.

[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Carry on with the paracetamol alongside it. Take the amoxicillin with a little food if it turns your stomach. Skip a heavy shift, though light work is fine if you feel up to it.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Amoxacillin, right. And if I can't swallow, or I can't get my breath, do I just wait for the dentist?
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Don't wait on that. If swallowing or breathing gets difficult, or the swelling jumps and you feel properly unwell, go straight to A&E or call 999.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): OK. Do I come back here as well, or only the dentist? Sorry, I know I'm asking a lot.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the swelling isn't down in forty-eight hours, come back and see me. Ring the dentist on Monday too, in case they get a cancellation.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Forty-eight hours. I'll go to the chemist now. Thank you.
[SEG0034] person_3 (NURSE): I'll get that prescription printed. Ignore my voice, my little boy's had a cold all week, so if I'm bunged up that's me, not you.

spec.situation: Cheek swelling and throbbing toothache for three days after a crown; fever mild; dentist unavailable; doctor prescribes antibiotic, warns about swallowing or breathing difficulty.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

bad.reason: Staff reports vomiting, but patient explicitly denies vomiting at all.
Doctor found no collection, but transcript does not locate it specifically to right cheek.

omissions.text: Vomiting was explicitly denied by the patient: 'I have not been vomiting, not once.' Recording vomiting as present/disputed misses the patient's clear negative symptom report.
Naproxen discontinuation detail missing: patient said she stopped naproxen in March because the GP took her off it, and the doctor confirmed to leave it stopped.
Metronidazole was discussed by the dentist but never prescribed/dispensed and the patient never took any; this is an important medication history clarification.
Examination finding/assessment detail missing: doctor stated he did not think the infection had tracked into the neck.
Amoxicillin counselling detail missing: start today and finish the course.
